title: Analysis & Visualizations
text:
Dashboard Pages

Page 1: Complaint Overview
Addresses Question 1: Does traffic volume correlate with complaint frequency?






Complaint Overview dashboard page showing street-related 311 complaints by borough and type, total complaint count (905,534), avg days to close (12), and a dual-axis chart of avg daily traffic per street segment vs. total complaints by borough.





Key findings:

Queens leads in total complaints (279,093), followed by Brooklyn (252,399), Manhattan (154,282), the Bronx (141,874), and Staten Island (77,886)
Manhattan has the highest average daily traffic (about 13,500 vehicles per counted street segment per day) but ranks 3rd in complaints. Staten Island ranks 2nd in traffic with the fewest complaints, and Queens has the most complaints with the 3rd highest traffic. The traffic ranking (Manhattan, Staten Island, Queens, Brooklyn, Bronx) does not match the complaint ranking, so traffic volume alone does not predict complaint frequency
Borough traffic averages rest on few counts (178 segment-days in Staten Island, 739 in Manhattan, 1,454 in Brooklyn), so the traffic ranking should be read with caution
Street Condition and Street Light Condition account for the majority of complaints across all boroughs



Page 2: Response Time Analysis
Addresses Question 2 and the T2R KPI: Does response time vary across boroughs, and does higher traffic lead to longer repair times?






Response Time Analysis page showing two Peak-Load KPI scorecards (avg days to close during peak vs. non-peak traffic months), avg days to close by borough bar chart, a sortable response time summary table, avg daily traffic volume by borough, and a dual-axis T2R chart comparing avg days to close against avg daily traffic volume by borough.





Key findings:

Brooklyn has the slowest avg response time (14.1 days); Staten Island the fastest (6.8 days). Manhattan (13.4), Queens (12.8), and the Bronx (10.4) fall in between
Queens has the most complaints (279,093) but ranks 3rd in response time (12.8 days), so a high complaint volume does not by itself mean slower closure
Peak-Load Service Lag KPI: Avg days to close is 12.66 days in peak traffic months and 12.69 days in non-peak months, and the median is 1 day in both groups. We found no difference. Peak months are defined with a within-segment traffic index (see Query 9), and months with fewer than 30 segment-days of counts are excluded
The T2R dual-axis chart shows no consistent pattern across the five boroughs. Staten Island has the 2nd highest traffic and the fastest closure, Manhattan has the highest traffic and the 2nd slowest closure, Brooklyn (4th in traffic) is the slowest, and the Bronx (lowest traffic) is the 2nd fastest. With five data points this is descriptive, not a statistical test



Page 3: Geographic & Temporal Patterns
Shows where street complaints concentrate (ZIP code) and when they are filed (seasonal pattern).






Geographic and temporal patterns page showing a choropleth map of complaint hotspots by ZIP code, a seasonal line chart by year, and a top ZIP code table.





Key findings:

The ZIP codes with the most street complaints are 10314 (Staten Island, 13,807), 11385 (Queens, 11,397), 10306 (Staten Island, 10,949), 11101 (Queens, 10,889), and 10312 (Staten Island, 10,825). Three of the top five ZIP codes are in Staten Island, the borough with the fewest complaints overall
These are raw counts. We have no population or street-mile denominator, so they show where complaints are concentrated, not which areas have the worst roads
91.2% of street complaints (825,575) have a valid ZIP code and appear on the map. 8.6% (78,254) have no ZIP code and 0.2% (1,705) carry the invalid placeholder “10000”; both groups are excluded from the map
Complaints tend to peak in late winter and spring (March was the peak month in 2022, 2023, and 2024) and reach their lowest point in November in every year from 2021 to 2025
2022 was the highest year (182,006 complaints) and 2020 the lowest (123,410), with a sharp drop in April 2020 (6,812 vs. 12,123 in March) that coincides with the COVID-19 lockdown

title: Analysis & Visualizations
text:
SQL Queries
All queries were run in BigQuery against the raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts dataset. Each CREATE TABLE version persists results as a mart table used directly by Looker Studio.

🔗 Full SQL file on GitHub or see queries/milestone5_queries.sql in this repository.



Method notes
Four checks shaped the final queries:

ZIP-level counts must reconcile to borough totals. dim_incident_location has repeated incident_location_key values, which duplicated complaints when the fact table was joined to it. Query 6 collapses the dimension to one row per key first. The corrected ZIP table totals 825,575 complaints, below the 905,534 borough total because null and “10000” ZIP codes are excluded.
Traffic is measured per street segment per day. The DOT counts only a few segments per borough on a given day (about 2.0 to 2.6 on average), so summing all counts in a borough-day mostly measures how many segments were counted. Queries 4, 5, 7, and 9 first sum vol to the segment-day, then average.
complaints_per_million_vehicles was removed. Its denominator reflected counting effort, not traffic, and produced extreme outliers in sparse months. Query 5 now reports monthly complaints next to average daily traffic per segment.
The analysis window is 2020 to 2025. The warehouse also holds complaints created in 2026 (38,861 street-related complaints) and some 2026 traffic counts. Every query now filters to 2020 through 2025, so all totals describe the same period.




Query 1: Complaints by Borough and Problem Type
Aggregation: borough × problem type
Purpose: Baseline complaint counts per borough → the foundation for cross-mart comparison with traffic volume.
SELECT
    l.borough                                           AS borough,
    p.problem_type                                      AS problem_type,
    COUNT(*)                                            AS total_complaints
FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_311service_request` f
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_location` l
    ON f.location_id = l.location_key
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_problem` p
    ON f.problem_id = p.problem_key
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
    ON f.created_date_id = d.date_key
WHERE p.problem_type IN (
    'Street Condition',
    'Street Light Condition',
    'Traffic Signal Condition',
    'Highway Condition',
    'DEP Highway Condition'
)
  AND d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
GROUP BY l.borough, p.problem_type
ORDER BY total_complaints DESC;



Query 2: Avg Response Time (Days to Close) by Borough
Aggregation: borough
Purpose: Answers Q2: Does borough response time vary? Uses two CTE date joins to compute DATE_DIFF between created_date and closed_date.
WITH created_dates AS (
    SELECT
        f.unique_key,
        f.location_id,
        f.problem_id,
        d.full_date                                     AS created_date
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_311service_request` f
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
        ON f.created_date_id = d.date_key
    WHERE d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
),
closed_dates AS (
    SELECT
        f.unique_key,
        d.full_date                                     AS closed_date
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_311service_request` f
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
        ON f.closed_date_id = d.date_key
)
SELECT
    l.borough,
    COUNT(*)                                            AS total_closed_requests,
    ROUND(AVG(DATE_DIFF(cl.closed_date,
              cr.created_date, DAY)), 2)                AS avg_days_to_close,
    MIN(DATE_DIFF(cl.closed_date,
        cr.created_date, DAY))                          AS min_days_to_close,
    MAX(DATE_DIFF(cl.closed_date,
        cr.created_date, DAY))                          AS max_days_to_close
FROM created_dates cr
INNER JOIN closed_dates cl      ON cr.unique_key = cl.unique_key
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_location` l
    ON cr.location_id = l.location_key
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_problem` p
    ON cr.problem_id = p.problem_key
WHERE p.problem_type IN (
    'Street Condition', 'Street Light Condition',
    'Traffic Signal Condition', 'Highway Condition', 'DEP Highway Condition'
)
  AND cl.closed_date >= cr.created_date   -- exclude data anomalies
GROUP BY l.borough
ORDER BY avg_days_to_close DESC;



Query 3: Monthly Complaint Trends by Year
Aggregation: year × month
Purpose: Identifies seasonal patterns in street infrastructure complaints. Used in cross-mart comparison with monthly traffic volume (Query 5).
SELECT
    d.year                                              AS complaint_year,
    d.month                                             AS complaint_month,
    COUNT(*)                                            AS total_complaints
FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_311service_request` f
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
    ON f.created_date_id = d.date_key
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_problem` p
    ON f.problem_id = p.problem_key
WHERE p.problem_type IN (
    'Street Condition', 'Street Light Condition',
    'Traffic Signal Condition', 'Highway Condition', 'DEP Highway Condition'
)
  AND d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
GROUP BY d.year, d.month
ORDER BY d.year, d.month;



Query 4: Avg Daily Traffic per Street Segment by Borough
Aggregation: borough
Purpose: Computes the borough-level average daily traffic from the 15-minute interval counts. Counts are first summed to one value per street segment per day, then averaged by borough. The result reads as “vehicles counted per segment per day.” Used as the traffic side of the cross-mart comparison.
WITH segment_day AS (
    SELECT
        f.location_id                                   AS location_id,
        f.segment_id                                    AS segment_id,
        d.full_date                                     AS traffic_date,
        SUM(f.vol)                                      AS daily_vol
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_traffic_volume` f
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
        ON f.date_id = d.date_key
    WHERE d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
    GROUP BY f.location_id, f.segment_id, d.full_date
)
SELECT
    l.borough                                           AS borough,
    COUNT(DISTINCT sd.traffic_date)                     AS days_measured,
    COUNT(*)                                            AS segment_days_measured,
    ROUND(AVG(sd.daily_vol), 0)                         AS avg_daily_traffic_volume
FROM segment_day sd
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_location` l
    ON sd.location_id = l.location_key
GROUP BY l.borough
ORDER BY avg_daily_traffic_volume DESC;
Result (2020 to 2025): Manhattan 13,496 (739 segment-days); Staten Island 12,258 (178); Queens 10,007 (1,179); Brooklyn 9,547 (1,454); Bronx 6,806 (639). Averages rest on few counts, so the ranking is sensitive to which segments were counted.



Query 5: Monthly Traffic vs. Complaints (Cross-Mart) ⭐
Aggregation: borough × year × month
Cross-mart: Joins fact_traffic_volume + fact_311service_request via conformed Dim_Date and Dim_Location.
Purpose: Core cross-mart query. Places monthly street complaints next to the monthly average of daily traffic per segment for each borough. The earlier complaints_per_million_vehicles ratio was removed because its denominator reflected how many segments were counted in a month, not how busy the roads were.
WITH segment_day AS (
    SELECT
        f.location_id                                   AS location_id,
        f.segment_id                                    AS segment_id,
        f.date_id                                       AS date_id,
        SUM(f.vol)                                      AS daily_vol
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_traffic_volume` f
    GROUP BY f.location_id, f.segment_id, f.date_id
),
monthly_traffic AS (
    SELECT
        l.borough,
        d.year,
        d.month,
        ROUND(AVG(sd.daily_vol), 0)                     AS avg_daily_traffic_per_segment
    FROM segment_day sd
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
        ON sd.date_id = d.date_key
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_location` l
        ON sd.location_id = l.location_key
    WHERE d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
    GROUP BY l.borough, d.year, d.month
),
monthly_complaints AS (
    SELECT
        l.borough,
        d.year,
        d.month,
        COUNT(*)                                        AS monthly_complaints
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_311service_request` f
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
        ON f.created_date_id = d.date_key
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_location` l
        ON f.location_id = l.location_key
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_problem` p
        ON f.problem_id = p.problem_key
    WHERE p.problem_type IN (
        'Street Condition', 'Street Light Condition',
        'Traffic Signal Condition', 'Highway Condition', 'DEP Highway Condition'
    )
      AND d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
    GROUP BY l.borough, d.year, d.month
)
SELECT
    mt.borough,
    mt.year,
    mt.month,
    mt.avg_daily_traffic_per_segment,
    mc.monthly_complaints                               AS monthly_street_complaints
FROM monthly_traffic mt
INNER JOIN monthly_complaints mc
    ON mt.borough = mc.borough
   AND mt.year    = mc.year
   AND mt.month   = mc.month
ORDER BY mt.borough, mt.year, mt.month;
Borough-months with no DOT traffic counts do not appear in this result.



Query 6: Complaints by ZIP Code (Choropleth Map)
Aggregation: zip code × borough × problem type
Purpose: Provides ZIP-code-level complaint counts for the choropleth map in Looker Studio, enabling geographic analysis beyond borough level.
Note: dim_incident_location contains repeated incident_location_key values, so it is collapsed to one row per key before the join. Without this step each complaint was counted once per repeated row and the ZIP totals exceeded the borough totals. Complaints with a null ZIP or the placeholder “10000” are excluded.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
  `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.complaints_by_zip_code`
AS
SELECT
    il.zip_code,
    l.borough,
    p.problem_type,
    COUNT(*)                                            AS total_complaints
FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_311service_request` f
INNER JOIN (
    -- dim_incident_location has duplicate keys (same ZIP on every copy),
    -- so collapse to one row per key before joining
    SELECT
        incident_location_key,
        ANY_VALUE(zip_code)                             AS zip_code
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_incident_location`
    GROUP BY incident_location_key
) il
    ON f.incident_location_id = il.incident_location_key
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_location` l
    ON f.location_id = l.location_key
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_problem` p
    ON f.problem_id = p.problem_key
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
    ON f.created_date_id = d.date_key
WHERE p.problem_type IN (
    'Street Condition', 'Street Light Condition',
    'Traffic Signal Condition', 'Highway Condition', 'DEP Highway Condition'
)
  AND d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
  AND il.zip_code IS NOT NULL
  AND il.zip_code != '10000'   -- placeholder, not a real ZIP code
GROUP BY il.zip_code, l.borough, p.problem_type
ORDER BY total_complaints DESC;
Reconciliation: the table totals 825,575 complaints. Adding 78,254 null-ZIP and 1,705 “10000” complaints gives 905,534, which matches the borough total from Query 1.



Query 7: Combined Traffic vs. Complaints by Borough (Cross-Mart) ⭐
Aggregation: borough
Cross-mart: Combines fact_traffic_volume + fact_311service_request.
Purpose: Single borough-level table for the dual-axis dashboard chart that directly addresses Q1. Traffic uses the same segment-day grain as Query 4.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
  `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.complaints_vs_traffic_by_borough`
AS
WITH segment_day AS (
    SELECT
        f.location_id                                   AS location_id,
        f.segment_id                                    AS segment_id,
        f.date_id                                       AS date_id,
        SUM(f.vol)                                      AS daily_vol
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_traffic_volume` f
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
        ON f.date_id = d.date_key
    WHERE d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
    GROUP BY f.location_id, f.segment_id, f.date_id
),
traffic AS (
    SELECT
        l.borough,
        ROUND(AVG(sd.daily_vol), 0)                     AS avg_daily_traffic_volume
    FROM segment_day sd
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_location` l
        ON sd.location_id = l.location_key
    GROUP BY l.borough
),
complaints AS (
    SELECT
        l.borough,
        COUNT(*)                                        AS total_complaints
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_311service_request` f
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_location` l
        ON f.location_id = l.location_key
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_problem` p
        ON f.problem_id = p.problem_key
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
        ON f.created_date_id = d.date_key
    WHERE p.problem_type IN (
        'Street Condition', 'Street Light Condition',
        'Traffic Signal Condition', 'Highway Condition', 'DEP Highway Condition'
    )
      AND d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
    GROUP BY l.borough
)
SELECT
    t.borough,
    t.avg_daily_traffic_volume,
    c.total_complaints
FROM traffic t
INNER JOIN complaints c ON t.borough = c.borough
ORDER BY t.avg_daily_traffic_volume DESC;



Query 8: Traffic-to-Repair Correlation (T2R) by Borough ⭐
Aggregation: borough
Cross-mart: Joins complaints_vs_traffic_by_borough + response_time_by_borough
Purpose: Directly addresses the T2R KPI: Does higher traffic volume go with slower repair times? Computes two derived metrics: traffic_per_repair_day (traffic absorbed per repair day) and complaints_per_repair_day (repair throughput). Powers the dual-axis T2R chart on the Response Time Analysis dashboard page. Run it after Queries 2 and 7, since it reads the tables they build. With five boroughs it is a descriptive comparison, not a statistical test.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
  `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.traffic_to_repair_correlation`
AS
SELECT
    t.borough,
    t.avg_daily_traffic_volume,
    t.total_complaints,
    r.avg_days_to_close,
    r.total_closed_requests,
    -- T2R metric: does higher traffic go with longer repair time?
    ROUND(t.avg_daily_traffic_volume /
          NULLIF(r.avg_days_to_close, 0), 2)            AS traffic_per_repair_day,
    -- Complaint resolution rate: complaints per day to close
    ROUND(t.total_complaints /
          NULLIF(r.avg_days_to_close, 0), 2)            AS complaints_per_repair_day
FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.complaints_vs_traffic_by_borough` t
INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.response_time_by_borough` r
    ON t.borough = r.borough
ORDER BY avg_daily_traffic_volume DESC;



Query 9: Peak-Load Service Lag KPI ⭐
Aggregation: traffic period (Peak vs. Non-Peak months)
Cross-mart: Joins fact_traffic_volume + fact_311service_request + dim_date + dim_problem
Purpose: Directly addresses the Peak-Load Service Lag KPI: Does avg time to close 311 complaints increase during months with above-average traffic? Each street segment is compared with its own average daily volume (a traffic index, where 1.0 is a typical day for that segment). A month is “Peak” when its average index is above the mean index across qualifying months in 2020 to 2025.
Why an index: the DOT counts only a few segments per month, so average raw volume swings with which segments were counted (for example, 31,046 in April 2023 vs. 5,983 in May 2023). The index removes that effect. Months with fewer than 30 segment-days of counts are excluded because a single segment can flip their label.
Finding: Peak months average 12.66 days to close and non-peak months 12.69 days (median 1 day in both). We observed no difference. The comparison is descriptive: no significance test was run and traffic counts are sparse, so this shows no evidence of a peak-load lag, not proof that none exists. (A first version using raw citywide volume showed 13.97 vs. 11.40 days, but that split was driven by which segments were counted.)
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
  `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.peak_load_service_lag`
AS
WITH segment_day AS (
    SELECT f.segment_id, f.date_id, SUM(f.vol)          AS daily_vol
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_traffic_volume` f
    GROUP BY f.segment_id, f.date_id
),
segment_avg AS (
    -- each segment's own typical daily volume
    SELECT segment_id, AVG(daily_vol)                   AS seg_avg
    FROM segment_day
    GROUP BY segment_id
),
monthly_index AS (
    -- 1.0 = counted segments at their own average; above 1.0 = busier than usual
    SELECT
        d.year,
        d.month,
        AVG(sd.daily_vol / NULLIF(sa.seg_avg, 0))       AS traffic_index,
        COUNT(*)                                        AS segment_days
    FROM segment_day sd
    INNER JOIN segment_avg sa ON sd.segment_id = sa.segment_id
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` d
        ON sd.date_id = d.date_key
    WHERE d.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
    GROUP BY d.year, d.month
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 30   -- drop months with too few counts to trust
),
peak_months AS (
    SELECT
        year,
        month,
        CASE
            WHEN traffic_index > (SELECT AVG(traffic_index) FROM monthly_index)
            THEN 'Peak'
            ELSE 'Non-Peak'
        END                                             AS traffic_period
    FROM monthly_index
),
response_times AS (
    SELECT
        cd.year,
        cd.month,
        DATE_DIFF(cl.full_date, cd.full_date, DAY)      AS days_to_close
    FROM `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.fact_311service_request` f
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` cd
        ON f.created_date_id = cd.date_key
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_date` cl
        ON f.closed_date_id = cl.date_key
    INNER JOIN `raul-cis-9440-spring2026.group_3_marts.dim_problem` p
        ON f.problem_id = p.problem_key
    WHERE p.problem_type IN (
        'Street Condition', 'Street Light Condition',
        'Traffic Signal Condition', 'Highway Condition', 'DEP Highway Condition'
    )
    AND cl.full_date >= cd.full_date
    AND cd.year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025
)
SELECT
    pm.traffic_period,
    COUNT(*)                                            AS total_requests,
    ROUND(AVG(CAST(rt.days_to_close AS FLOAT64)), 2)   AS avg_days_to_close,
    APPROX_QUANTILES(rt.days_to_close, 100)[OFFSET(50)] AS median_days_to_close,
    MIN(rt.days_to_close)                               AS min_days_to_close,
    MAX(rt.days_to_close)                               AS max_days_to_close
FROM response_times rt
INNER JOIN peak_months pm
    ON rt.year = pm.year AND rt.month = pm.month
GROUP BY pm.traffic_period
ORDER BY pm.traffic_period;

title: Dimensional Model
text:
Design Decisions & Notes






Tip



Why separate Dim_Incident_Location from Dim_Location?
Dim_Location is a conformed, low-cardinality borough-level dimension shared with the traffic mart. Dim_Incident_Location holds high-cardinality address-level data specific to 311 requests, preventing fact table bloat and preserving the conformed dimension’s reusability.








Tip



Multiple date foreign keys on the fact table
Each 311 request has three relevant dates: created, closed, and due. Rather than using a single date dimension, three foreign keys point to the same Dim_Date table, a standard Kimball role-playing dimension pattern.








Warning



Known data issue: duplicate keys in Dim_Incident_Location
In the built warehouse table (dim_incident_location), the key column incident_location_key is not unique: several rows share the same key, and each copy carries the same ZIP code. Joining the 311 fact table straight to this dimension repeats each complaint once per copy. This inflated the first version of the ZIP-level counts (Query 6) above the true borough totals. Query 6 now collapses the dimension to one row per key before joining, and the ZIP table reconciles to the borough totals. A unique test on this key should be added to the dbt project so the duplicates are caught at build time.
The model diagram shows logical column names (incident_location_id, incident_zip_code). The built table uses incident_location_key and zip_code.








Note



Analysis grain for traffic
The traffic fact table stores 15-minute counts per segment and direction. The DOT counts only a few segments per borough on a given day, so the analysis queries first sum vol to one value per segment per day and then average across those segment-days. Summing across every segment counted in a borough-day would reward boroughs that simply had more segments counted.








Warning



Known challenge: geographic join between marts
The 311 data provides borough + zip code, while the traffic data provides a road segment + WKT geometry. Cross-mart geographic joins are therefore at the borough level rather than street-segment level. This is noted as a limitation in the Conclusion section.

title: NYC Traffic & Road Infrastructure Analysis
text:
Introduction
New York City’s road infrastructure handles some of the highest traffic volumes in the United States. When roads degrade, potholes form, traffic signals fail, street lights go dark, and the burden falls on residents, delivery networks, and emergency services alike. Yet maintenance resources are finite, and response times vary widely across boroughs.
This project builds a data warehouse that integrates two NYC Open Data sources to investigate whether traffic volume is a meaningful predictor of infrastructure complaints, and whether boroughs with higher traffic also experience slower repair response times.

Analytics Questions

Q1: Does traffic volume correlate with complaint frequency?
To what extent does high traffic volume (specifically heavy vehicle counts) correlate with the frequency of “Street Condition,” “Street Light Condition,” and related 311 complaints?


Q2: Does response time vary across boroughs?
How does agency response time for road repairs vary between high-traffic zones and low-traffic zones? Is there a measurable “maintenance lag” in high-traffic areas?



Key Metrics / KPIs







KPI
Description




Pothole Incidence Rate (PIR)
Total “Street Condition” complaints ÷ avg daily traffic volume per segment


Traffic-to-Repair Correlation (T2R)
Do higher traffic volumes go with faster or slower resolution? Computed at the borough level (five data points), so it is a descriptive comparison, not a statistical test


Peak-Load Service Lag
Avg days-to-close in peak traffic months vs. non-peak months, where “peak” means the counted street segments were busier than their own average





Data Sources



Source
Description
Link




NYC 311 Service Requests
Community-reported road/infrastructure issues, filtered to street-related complaint types, 2020-2025
NYC Open Data


DOT Automatic Traffic Volume Counts
15-minute interval automated traffic counts at DOT sensor locations, 2020-2025
NYC Open Data





Potential Stakeholders

NYC Department of Transportation (DOT): prioritize preventive maintenance on high-traffic / low-complaint roads before failure occurs.
Logistics & Delivery Companies: identify high-incident routes that increase vehicle maintenance costs or delivery delays.
Urban Planners: assess whether current road materials are sufficient for the actual traffic load detected by sensors.

Reproducibility
To reproduce the full pipeline from scratch:

Clone the GitHub repository
Set up a BigQuery project and configure profiles.yml with your credentials
Run the Cloud Function (or equivalent) to load raw data
From the repo root: dbt deps && dbt run && dbt test
Run the Milestone 5 SQL queries (queries/milestone5_queries.sql) in BigQuery to create the analytics mart tables used by Looker Studio. The tables are built with CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, so rerunning refreshes them. Run order matters because Query 8 reads tables built by Queries 2 and 7: the Query 1, 2 and 3 tables, then Query 6, 4, 7, 5, 8, 9.


Data quality note
dim_incident_location contains repeated values of incident_location_key. The analysis queries handle this by collapsing the dimension to one row per key before joining (see Query 6). Adding a dbt unique test on that key is the recommended fix at the pipeline level.

title: Conclusion & Results
text:
This project set out to answer two core analytics questions about NYC road infrastructure using a data warehouse integrating 311 service requests and DOT automated traffic volume counts from 2020 to 2025.


At the borough level, we found no clear relationship. Manhattan carries the highest average daily traffic (about 13,500 vehicles per counted street segment per day) yet ranks third in total complaints (154,282). Staten Island has the second highest traffic (about 12,300) and the fewest complaints (77,886), while Queens has the most complaints (279,093) with the third highest traffic (about 10,000). Across the five boroughs, the traffic ranking and the complaint ranking do not match.
The traffic comparison deserves caution. The DOT counted only a small number of segments, so each borough’s average rests on few observations (178 segment-days in Staten Island, 639 in the Bronx, 739 in Manhattan, 1,179 in Queens, and 1,454 in Brooklyn), and a different set of counted segments could reorder the boroughs.
This suggests that raw traffic volume is an incomplete predictor of complaint frequency. Other factors, including road age, lane miles, residential density, and reporting behavior, likely contribute, but this project did not test them.
The T2R metric (Query 8) and Peak-Load Service Lag KPI (Query 9) point the same way. Days to close shows no consistent pattern with traffic: Staten Island has the second highest traffic and the fastest closure, Brooklyn (fourth in traffic) is the slowest, and the Bronx (lowest traffic) is the second fastest. Five data points cannot support a statistical claim. For peak load, we defined peak months with a within-segment traffic index so that the result does not depend on which segments the DOT happened to count. Average closure time was 12.66 days in peak months and 12.69 days in non-peak months, with a median of 1 day in both. We observed no difference, which is not the same as proving that no lag exists, because the traffic counts are sparse and no significance test was run.



Yes. Brooklyn takes an average of 14.1 days to close a street complaint, followed by Manhattan (13.4), Queens (12.8), and the Bronx (10.4). Staten Island closes in just 6.8 days, about half of Brooklyn’s time.
Staten Island has the fewest complaints of any borough, yet three of its ZIP codes (10314, 10306, and 10312) are in the citywide top five by complaint count. Because those are raw counts with no population or street-mile denominator, they show where complaints concentrate, not where roads are worst.
The Staten Island result is worth highlighting: it has the second highest measured traffic and the fastest closure time, the opposite of a traffic-driven lag. Whether the differences reflect staffing, complaint types, or geographic compactness requires further investigation.
Averages also hide how skewed closure times are. In the Query 9 sample the median was 1 day while the average was about 12.7 days, because a minority of tickets stay open for a very long time (the longest exceeded 1,900 days).

title: Conclusion & Results
text:
Recommendations for Stakeholders
For the NYC Department of Transportation:

Investigate why Brooklyn has the slowest average closure time (14.1 days) while ranking second in total complaints. A borough-level staffing or routing analysis could identify whether this is a resource or workflow issue.
Review Staten Island ZIP codes 10314, 10306, and 10312, which are in the citywide top five by complaint count. Check complaint rates per street mile or household before prioritizing preventive maintenance, since our counts are not normalized.
The seasonal chart shows complaints peaking in late winter and spring (March was the peak month in 2022, 2023, and 2024), which suggests that seasonal readiness planning (winter road damage followed by a spring complaint wave) could reduce peak workload.

For Logistics & Delivery Companies:

Queens ZIP codes 11385 and 11101 have among the highest complaint counts in the city (11,397 and 10,889). Route planning tools that incorporate 311 complaint hotspot data could help reduce vehicle maintenance costs and delays.

For Urban Planners:

The disconnect between traffic sensor coverage and complaint geography highlights a data gap: traffic sensors are concentrated in certain corridors, while complaints span the full residential street network. Expanding sensor coverage to residential ZIP codes with high complaint counts would enable more precise infrastructure planning.

title: Conclusion & Results
text:
Limitations & Data Challenges






Warning



Geographic join resolution
The 311 data geolocates complaints to ZIP codes, while the traffic data geolocates sensors to road segments with WKT geometries. Cross-mart joins are therefore only possible at the borough level, not at the street or ZIP level. A more granular spatial join (e.g., snapping complaints to the nearest sensor segment) was out of scope for this project but would substantially strengthen the analysis.








Warning



Traffic sensor coverage is sparse and uneven
The DOT traffic count dataset covers a subset of road segments, not the full street network, and only a few segments are counted in a borough on a given day (about 2.0 to 2.6 on average). Sensors are more densely placed on arterial and commercial roads, so residential streets, which generate many of the complaints in outer-borough ZIP codes, may be systematically under-counted. Because of this, traffic is measured as the average count per street segment per day, borough averages rest on as few as 178 segment-days (Staten Island), and some months have too few counts to use (Query 9 excludes months with fewer than 30 segment-days). Borough traffic rankings should therefore be treated as indicative only.








Note



Traffic counts do not cover the full period
The DOT records traffic at specific segments for specific periods; not all segments are counted every day, and several months in 2020 have no counts at all. The average daily traffic figures used in this analysis are averages over counted segment-days only, which may introduce bias toward the periods and streets the DOT chose to measure.








Note



Analysis window
All results cover complaints and traffic counts from 2020 through 2025. The extracts also contained 2026 records (38,861 street-related complaints at the time of extraction), which were excluded so that every figure describes the same six years.








Note



Missing ZIP codes
8.6% of street complaints (78,254) have no ZIP code and 0.2% (1,705) carry the invalid placeholder “10000”. Both are excluded from the ZIP-level map and rankings, which cover 91.2% of complaints (825,575). A first version of the ZIP query double-counted complaints because dim_incident_location has repeated keys; the final query de-duplicates the dimension, and the ZIP table now reconciles to the borough totals.








Note



311 reporting behavior varies by community
Complaint counts reflect both actual infrastructure conditions and the willingness of residents to file 311 reports. Areas with higher civic engagement may show more complaints not because their roads are worse, but because residents are more likely to report issues.








Note



Five boroughs, no significance testing
Borough-level comparisons rest on five data points, and no statistical tests were run. The findings are descriptive.

title: Conclusion & Results
text:
Recommended Follow-Up Analysis

Street-segment level spatial join: Use PostGIS or BigQuery GIS functions to snap 311 complaints to their nearest DOT sensor segment, enabling correlation analysis at a finer geographic grain.
Complaint type decomposition: Analyze whether Street Condition complaints (a category that includes potholes among other defects) track differently from Street Light Condition complaints relative to traffic volume, since road surface damage is more directly caused by vehicle load.
Year-over-year response time trend: Query 2 produces a static borough average. Adding a year dimension would show whether response times are improving or degrading over the 2020–2025 window.
Heavy vehicle sub-analysis: The original proposal targeted heavy vehicle counts (trucks) specifically. The DOT dataset includes vehicle class data that was not fully leveraged here; a filtered analysis on heavy vehicles vs. road surface complaints would better test the infrastructure-degradation hypothesis.
Normalized complaint rates: Divide ZIP-level complaint counts by street miles or households so that ZIP codes can be compared on rate, not just on volume.
